---
title: "Snapshot summaries"
toc: true
---

The simplest dynamic analysis is often to calculate ordinary persistence
separately at selected times or windows. At each physical time $t$,

$$
X_t\longrightarrow K_{\varepsilon,t}
\longrightarrow H_p(K_{\varepsilon,t})
\longrightarrow D_t.
$$

The filtration scale $\varepsilon$ varies within one snapshot. Physical time
$t$ changes the snapshot. Keeping those axes separate prevents a sequence of
static calculations from being mistaken for persistence through time.

::: {.column-margin .study-note .insight}
**What snapshots can claim.** A sequence $D_t$ records change in summaries.
It does not identify a class in one diagram with a class in the next.
:::

## Choose the snapshot object

A moving system may supply positions, states, interactions, images or a
scalar signal. These lead respectively to point clouds, graphs, cubical
complexes or filtered functions. The representation decides what a component
or hole means before any dynamic summary is calculated.

::: {.column-margin .study-note .audience-dynamics}
**A scalar signal offers several questions.** A direct sublevel filtration
studies connected low-valued runs. A delay-coordinate embedding can instead
turn successive signal values into a state-space point cloud and expose
recurrence. Lag, embedding dimension and window length then become additional
modelling choices [@perea2015sw1pers].
:::

## Dynamic point clouds

A dynamic point cloud is a family

$$
\{X_t\}_{t\in T},
\qquad X_t=\{x_1(t),\ldots,x_{n_t}(t)\}.
$$

Writing $x_i(t)$ is appropriate only when observation $i$ is genuinely
tracked. For unlabelled snapshots, write $X_t$ without persistent point
indices. Timestamp order does not imply $X_t\subseteq X_{t+1}$, because the
points normally move or are replaced.

At each fixed $t$, a Rips construction produces $K_{\varepsilon,t}$ across
filtration scale. Ordinary persistence then produces $D_t$. This is a family
of static calculations indexed by time, not a persistence module in the time
direction.

Three snapshot summaries answer increasingly multiscale questions:

- the diagrams $D_t$, or distances between them, retain the birth-death
  configuration at each time;
- fixing $\varepsilon$ gives the Betti series
  $t\mapsto\beta_p(K_{\varepsilon,t})$;
- retaining both axes gives the Betti surface
  $C_p(t,\varepsilon)=\beta_p(K_{\varepsilon,t})$.

Diagram distances quantify change in complete diagrams but do not say which
class moved. A fixed-scale series is easy to compare with energy,
polarisation or rotation but depends on one defensible scale. A Betti surface
shows counts across time and scale without choosing one $\varepsilon$.

## Betti surfaces and CROCKER displays

For intervals $[b,d)$ in the degree-$p$ snapshot barcode at time $t$,

$$
C_p(t,\varepsilon)
=\#\{[b,d):b\leq\varepsilon<d\}.
$$

The symbol $\#$ means the number of intervals in the set. Thus
$C_p(t,\varepsilon)$ is exactly the snapshot Betti number at that scale.

One vertical slice is the Betti curve of one snapshot. One horizontal slice
shows how the count at a selected scale changes through physical time. Topaz,
Ziegelmeier and Halverson introduced CROCKER plots for biological aggregation
models [@topaz2015aggregation]. Xian and collaborators developed related
time-varying summaries and CROCKER stacks [@xian2022dynamics].

:::: {.worked-example}
### Read a CROCKER display from its slices

<iframe class="crocker-swarm-explorer"
src="../../assets/topic07-crocker-swarm.html"
title="A controlled dynamic point cloud beside its CROCKER matrix and selected slices"
loading="lazy"></iframe>

The balls have radius $\varepsilon/2$. Their overlaps show the selected Rips
edge threshold in the point cloud. Fix time and read vertically for one Betti
curve; fix scale and read horizontally for the count through time. The points
follow prescribed paths, so this is a checkable teaching example rather than
a biological model.
::::

CROCKER stacks add a persistence threshold as another display coordinate,
allowing short intervals to be suppressed [@xian2022dynamics]. That threshold
has the same interpretation burden as any other lifetime cutoff.

## Diagram stacks

Stacking diagrams in birth-death-time space can make possible trajectories
visible. Once a past diagram is computed, its plane and points should remain
fixed; new diagrams extend the stack.

:::: {.worked-example}
### A changing point cloud and diagram stack

<iframe class="dynamic-persistence-explorer"
src="../../assets/topic07-dynamic-persistence-explorer.html"
title="A changing point cloud, its current persistence diagram and a growing stack"
loading="lazy"></iframe>

The same changing point cloud is shown at the selected $\varepsilon$ beside
its current diagram. Each completed diagram remains fixed when a new layer is
added to the stack.
::::

::: {.column-margin .study-note .qualification}
**A stack is not tracking.** Joining nearby points on adjacent layers is a
visual or optimisation rule. A vineyard instead follows persistence pairings
along a specified path of changing filtrations.
:::

Windows are part of the observation model. Short windows may not contain
enough observations to support the expected structure; long windows may mix
regimes. Overlapping windows share data, so a smooth summary curve is not
independent evidence of slowly changing dynamics. Report the window rule,
representation, metric, filtration, coefficient field, homology degree and
dynamic summary.

::: {.checkpoint-route}

You are ready to continue when you can write the two-parameter object
$K_{\varepsilon,t}$ without confusing its axes, construct a CROCKER entry from
a barcode, identify the extra choices introduced by windows and distinguish a
stacked diagram from a vineyard.

:::
